The model rests on simplifying assumptions, including full employment, perfect competition, costless movement of resources between industries within a country, and the absence of transport costs. Critics argue that these assumptions can understate adjustment costs and that some countries may become locked into low-productivity specializations. Some economists also argue that temporary protection of infant industries can help develop new comparative advantages. Nevertheless, the core lesson that opportunity costs, rather than absolute productivity, determine the pattern of mutually beneficial trade remains widely accepted.
summary:
Ricardo's principle of comparative advantage shows that countries can gain from specialization and trade even when one is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources, but trade gains depend on comparative advantage—lower opportunity cost. In the example, country A has an absolute advantage in both cloth and wheat but a comparative advantage in cloth (wheat costs it 2 cloth), while country B has a comparative advantage in wheat (costing it 1 cloth). Specializing and trading at terms between 1 and 2 cloth per wheat, such as 1.5, benefits both, raising world output and allowing consumption beyond each production possibilities frontier.

The Ricardian model attributes comparative advantage to productivity differences, while the Heckscher-Ohlin model links it to factor endowments, predicting that labour-abundant countries such as Bangladesh export labour-intensive goods like garments. Trade creates winners and losers: the Stolper-Samuelson theorem predicts gains for abundant factors and losses for scarce ones, so retraining and social protection matter. Comparative advantage changes with capital, education, technology, scale economies, and learning, and modern theory explains intra-industry trade and specialization in tasks within global value chains. The model's assumptions—full employment, perfect competition, costless resource movement, and no transport costs—are criticized, and infant-industry arguments exist, but the opportunity-cost insight remains widely accepted.

source_text:
Managers frequently ask why some employees work hard while others with similar abilities do not. Content theories of motivation, such as Maslow's hierarchy of needs, focus on what people need. Process theories instead examine how people decide how much effort to exert. Victor Vroom's expectancy theory, proposed in 1964, is one of the most widely studied process theories. It holds that people choose their level of effort by considering whether effort will lead to performance, whether performance will lead to outcomes, and how much they value those outcomes. Motivation is therefore viewed as the result of rational, though often informal, calculations about the future.

Expectancy theory has three core components. Expectancy is the person's belief about the probability that putting in effort will result in successful performance. It ranges from zero, when a person believes that no amount of effort will achieve the required performance, to one, when the person is certain that effort will succeed. Expectancy is influenced by self-confidence, past experience, skills, the difficulty of the task, and the availability of resources and support. An employee asked to meet a sales target in a declining market without adequate training may have low expectancy.

Instrumentality is the belief that successful performance will lead to particular outcomes, such as a bonus, promotion, recognition, or, negatively, criticism and extra workload. It reflects the perceived link between performance and rewards. Instrumentality is low when employees believe that rewards are distributed according to favouritism, seniority, or chance rather than performance, or when the organization has a history of failing to keep promises. Clear, consistently applied reward systems tend to increase instrumentality.

Valence is the value that a person attaches to an outcome. Valence can be positive, when the outcome is desired; negative, when the outcome is something the person wants to avoid; or zero, when the person is indifferent. Valence differs among individuals. A promotion that requires relocation may have high positive valence for one employee and negative valence for another whose family commitments make moving undesirable. Time off may be highly valued by some employees and less important to others who prefer extra income.

Vroom expressed motivation, or motivational force, as a function of these components, often summarized as motivation equals expectancy multiplied by instrumentality multiplied by valence, summed across the outcomes associated with performance. The multiplicative form has an important implication: if any one component is close to zero, overall motivation will be low, no matter how high the others are. An employee may greatly value a bonus and believe that performance would be rewarded, but if the employee believes the target is unattainable, motivation will remain weak. Similarly, confidence and attainable targets do not motivate if rewards are not linked to performance or are not valued.

The theory has clear practical implications. To raise expectancy, managers can set challenging but achievable goals, provide training and coaching, ensure that employees have the necessary tools, information, and authority, and offer feedback that builds confidence. To raise instrumentality, they can clarify the criteria on which rewards are based, measure performance accurately and transparently, and consistently deliver promised rewards. To align valence, they can learn what different employees value and, where possible, offer rewards that match those preferences, for example through flexible benefit plans or choices between financial and non-financial recognition. The theory also warns that poorly designed incentive schemes, such as those that reward easily measured outcomes while neglecting quality, may motivate effort in the wrong direction.

Expectancy theory has been extended in several ways. Porter and Lawler's model added the roles of ability and role perceptions, arguing that effort leads to performance only if the person has the ability and understands what is expected. They also emphasised that satisfaction follows performance when rewards are perceived as fair, linking expectancy theory with equity considerations. Research has generally supported the importance of each component, especially for predicting choices between tasks and levels of effort.

The theory also faces criticism. It assumes that people make conscious, rational calculations, whereas real decisions are often influenced by habits, emotions, social norms, and limited information. Measuring expectancy, instrumentality, and valence precisely is difficult, and the multiplicative formula is not always supported by data. The theory is better at explaining differences in effort among options than at predicting absolute levels of motivation. Despite these limitations, it remains a useful diagnostic tool, because it directs managers to examine where the chain between effort, performance, and valued outcomes may be broken.
summary:
Vroom's expectancy theory is a process theory of motivation proposing that people choose effort based on whether effort leads to performance, whether performance leads to outcomes, and how much those outcomes are valued. Expectancy is the perceived probability that effort will produce performance, shaped by confidence, skills, task difficulty, and resources. Instrumentality is the belief that performance will bring outcomes such as bonuses or promotion, weakened when rewards seem based on favouritism or broken promises. Valence is the positive, negative, or neutral value a person places on an outcome and varies between individuals.

Motivation is often expressed as expectancy × instrumentality × valence summed across outcomes, so if any component is near zero, motivation is low. Managers can raise expectancy with achievable goals, training, resources, and feedback; raise instrumentality with clear, accurate, consistently applied reward systems; and align valence by offering rewards employees value, while avoiding incentives that reward the wrong behaviour. Porter and Lawler extended the theory with ability, role perceptions, and perceived fairness of rewards. Critics note its assumption of rational calculation, measurement difficulties, and inconsistent support for the multiplicative form, but it remains a useful tool for finding breaks in the effort-performance-reward chain.

source_text:
Educators need a shared language for describing what students are expected to learn. Bloom's taxonomy, first published in 1956 by a committee led by Benjamin Bloom, provided such a language by classifying educational objectives in the cognitive domain into a hierarchy of levels. The taxonomy was originally intended to help university examiners exchange test items and design assessments, but it became widely used in curriculum planning, lesson design, and teacher education around the world.

The original taxonomy described six major categories: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation. These categories were arranged from simple to complex and from concrete to abstract, and the framework assumed that mastery of each level depended on mastery of the levels below it. Knowledge referred to the recall of facts, terms, and methods. Comprehension involved understanding meaning, for example by translating or interpreting information. Application meant using knowledge in new situations. Analysis involved breaking material into parts and identifying relationships, synthesis involved combining elements to form a new whole, and evaluation involved making judgements based on criteria.

In 2001, Lorin Anderson and David Krathwohl, together with other cognitive psychologists, curriculum theorists, and assessment specialists, published a revised taxonomy. The revision made several important changes. The category names were changed from nouns to verbs, reflecting the idea that objectives describe what learners do: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, and create. The top two levels were reordered, so that create, which corresponds roughly to the original synthesis, became the highest level, above evaluate. The revisers argued that generating new ideas or products is generally more cognitively complex than judging existing ones. The strict cumulative hierarchy was also relaxed, recognizing that the categories may overlap and that learners do not always move through them in a fixed order.

The revised framework added a second dimension, the knowledge dimension, which classifies the type of knowledge involved. Factual knowledge consists of basic elements such as terminology and specific details. Conceptual knowledge involves relationships among elements, such as classifications, principles, theories, and models. Procedural knowledge concerns how to do something, including skills, techniques, methods, and criteria for when to use them. Metacognitive knowledge is awareness of one's own cognition, including knowledge of strategies, of task demands, and of oneself as a learner. Combining the cognitive process dimension and the knowledge dimension produces a two-dimensional taxonomy table, in which any objective can be located according to both the cognitive process and the type of knowledge it targets.

Each cognitive process category contains more specific processes. Remembering includes recognizing and recalling. Understanding includes interpreting, exemplifying, classifying, summarizing, inferring, comparing, and explaining. Applying includes executing a familiar procedure and implementing a procedure in an unfamiliar task. Analysing includes differentiating relevant from irrelevant information, organizing elements into a structure, and attributing a point of view or purpose. Evaluating includes checking for internal consistency and critiquing against external criteria. Creating includes generating hypotheses, planning a procedure, and producing a new product.

The taxonomy is used in several practical ways. When writing learning outcomes, teachers choose action verbs that correspond to the intended level, such as list for remembering, explain for understanding, calculate for applying, compare for analysing, justify for evaluating, and design for creating. Teachers then align teaching activities and assessments with these outcomes, a principle known as constructive alignment. If a course objective requires students to evaluate competing theories, but the examination asks only for definitions, the assessment is misaligned. The taxonomy also helps teachers check whether their questions and tasks are concentrated at lower levels and to plan activities that develop higher-order thinking.

Several cautions apply to the use of the taxonomy. Action verbs are not reliable indicators on their own; the cognitive demand of a task depends on what students must actually do and on what they have previously learned. A question beginning with explain may require only recall if the explanation was memorized from the textbook. Classifying tasks can be subjective, and different experts may assign the same item to different levels. The taxonomy should not be interpreted to mean that lower-level learning is unimportant: understanding and applying knowledge depend on accurate factual and conceptual foundations. Finally, the cognitive domain does not capture affective and psychomotor learning, for which separate taxonomies were developed.
summary:
Bloom's taxonomy, published in 1956, classifies cognitive educational objectives into a hierarchy originally named knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation, with each level assumed to build on those below. It was designed to help examiners share test items and became widely used in curriculum and assessment design.

Anderson and Krathwohl's 2001 revision renamed the categories as verbs—remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, and create—placed create above evaluate, and relaxed the strict hierarchy. It added a knowledge dimension of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge, producing a two-dimensional taxonomy table, and defined specific processes within each category, such as interpreting and explaining for understanding, differentiating and attributing for analysing, checking and critiquing for evaluating, and generating, planning, and producing for creating. Teachers use level-appropriate verbs to write outcomes and align activities and assessments through constructive alignment, avoiding mismatches such as testing only definitions for an evaluation objective, and use the taxonomy to balance lower- and higher-order tasks. However, verbs alone do not determine cognitive demand, classification can be subjective, lower-level knowledge remains essential, and affective and psychomotor learning require separate taxonomies.

source_text:
Vernacular architecture refers to buildings designed and constructed by local communities using traditional knowledge, locally available materials, and techniques refined over generations, usually without professional architects. In Bangladesh, a deltaic country with a hot and humid monsoon climate, frequent flooding, and limited stone resources, vernacular buildings have developed distinctive forms that respond closely to environmental conditions, social organization, and economic constraints. Studying these traditions provides lessons for contemporary sustainable and climate-responsive design.

The physical environment shapes vernacular building in fundamental ways. Bangladesh lies largely on the floodplains of the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers, where land is flat and soils are alluvial. Annual monsoon rains are heavy, and many areas experience seasonal flooding, while coastal regions face cyclones and storm surges. Temperatures and humidity are high for much of the year. Natural stone is scarce in most of the country, but clay, bamboo, timber, jute stalks, thatching grasses, and palm leaves are widely available. These conditions have produced buildings that are light, permeable, raised above flood levels, and quick to repair.

The rural homestead, or bari, is the basic unit of settlement. A typical homestead consists of several separate structures arranged around a central courtyard, called an uthan, on a plinth of earth raised above the surrounding fields. The raised plinth is created by excavating earth from a nearby pond, which then serves for bathing, washing, fish culture, and water storage. The courtyard acts as an outdoor living and working space where crops are dried and processed, children play, and social activities take place. Separate structures are used for sleeping, cooking, storage, and livestock, and the arrangement often reflects the joint family system, with new rooms added as the family grows. Trees around the homestead provide shade, fruit, timber, and protection from wind.

Construction materials and techniques vary by region. Mud houses, built with walls of compacted earth or mud blocks, are common in areas with suitable clay soils, such as parts of the northern and western regions. Thick mud walls provide thermal mass that moderates indoor temperature, keeping interiors cooler during hot days. Bamboo is perhaps the most important vernacular material. It is used for structural frames, wall panels woven into mats, roof structures, and floors in raised houses. Bamboo is strong, flexible, lightweight, and rapidly renewable, though untreated bamboo is vulnerable to insects and decay. In wetter regions and along rivers, houses may have walls of woven bamboo, jute stalks, or reeds, which allow air to pass through and dry quickly after rain.

Roofs are among the most characteristic elements of Bangladeshi vernacular architecture. Steeply pitched thatched roofs, made from rice straw, sungrass, or palm leaves, shed heavy monsoon rains quickly and provide good insulation against heat. The curved roof form known as the do-chala, a two-sided roof with a curved ridge and eaves, and the four-sided char-chala became so closely associated with Bengal that they were later adapted in brick temples and mosques and influenced Mughal architecture in the subcontinent. Wide overhanging eaves protect walls from rain and shade them from the sun. In recent decades, corrugated galvanized iron sheets have widely replaced thatch because of their durability and lower maintenance, although they absorb heat and make interiors hotter and noisier during rain.

Climatic responsiveness is visible in several design strategies. Buildings are often oriented to capture prevailing southerly breezes, and openings, verandas, and permeable walls support cross-ventilation, which is essential for comfort in humid conditions. Verandas, or semi-open transitional spaces, provide shaded areas for daily activities and protect the interior from rain and sun. Raised floors and plinths reduce damage from floods and dampness. In flood-prone char lands, the unstable river islands, houses are frequently designed to be dismantled and moved when erosion threatens, with bamboo frames and panels that can be reassembled elsewhere. In the coastal belt, some communities have adopted raised houses and stronger connections to reduce cyclone damage.

Vernacular architecture in Bangladesh faces significant pressures. Rapid population growth, rising land values, and urbanization encourage brick and concrete construction, which is often perceived as modern and durable. Traditional skills are declining as younger generations move away from rural crafts, and natural materials such as good-quality thatch and timber have become scarcer. At the same time, vernacular buildings have weaknesses, including vulnerability to floods, fire, and decay, and limited sanitation. Contemporary architects and researchers increasingly seek to combine the climatic intelligence and low environmental impact of vernacular traditions with improvements such as treated bamboo, stabilized earth blocks, better foundations, and improved water and sanitation facilities, creating housing that is both culturally appropriate and resilient.
summary:
Vernacular architecture in Bangladesh consists of community-built structures using local materials and traditional knowledge adapted to a flat deltaic floodplain, heavy monsoon rains, flooding, cyclones, heat, humidity, and scarce stone. Buildings are typically light, permeable, raised above flood levels, and easy to repair, using clay, bamboo, timber, jute stalks, grasses, and palm leaves. The rural homestead, or bari, groups separate sleeping, cooking, storage, and livestock structures around a courtyard (uthan) on a raised earth plinth formed by digging a pond, reflecting joint family life and surrounded by productive trees.

Mud walls provide thermal mass in clay-rich regions, while bamboo serves for frames, woven walls, roofs, and floors, and permeable reed or jute walls suit wetter areas. Steep thatched roofs shed rain and insulate, and the curved do-chala and char-chala forms influenced later temples, mosques, and Mughal architecture; corrugated iron now often replaces thatch despite being hotter and noisier. Orientation to southerly breezes, verandas, cross-ventilation, raised floors, movable houses on char lands, and raised coastal houses demonstrate climatic adaptation. Urbanization, preference for brick and concrete, declining craft skills, and scarce materials threaten these traditions, and vernacular buildings have flood, fire, decay, and sanitation weaknesses, so contemporary practice combines vernacular principles with treated bamboo, stabilized earth, better foundations, and improved sanitation.

Researchers often need to decide whether an observed pattern in data reflects a real effect or could plausibly have arisen by chance. A new teaching method may appear to raise examination scores, or a drug may seem to lower blood pressure, but random variation between samples can produce apparent differences even when there is no true effect. Statistical hypothesis testing provides a formal framework for assessing such evidence.

A test begins with two competing statements about a population parameter. The null hypothesis, written H0, usually states that there is no effect or no difference, for example that the mean blood pressure reduction under the drug equals that under placebo. The alternative hypothesis, H1 or Ha, states what the researcher seeks evidence for, such as that the drug produces a greater reduction. Alternatives may be one-sided, specifying a direction, or two-sided, allowing a difference in either direction. The choice should be made before examining the data, based on the research question.

The researcher then calculates a test statistic, a number that summarizes how far the sample results deviate from what the null hypothesis predicts, scaled by the variability expected from sampling. Common examples include the z statistic and t statistic for means and proportions, the chi-square statistic for categorical data, and the F statistic in analysis of variance. Under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true, the test statistic follows a known sampling distribution, which makes it possible to judge whether the observed value is unusual.

The p-value is the probability, calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed. A small p-value indicates that the observed data would be surprising if the null hypothesis were true, and is therefore regarded as evidence against it. Before conducting the test, researchers usually choose a significance level, alpha, commonly 0.05. If the p-value is less than or equal to alpha, the result is described as statistically significant and the null hypothesis is rejected; otherwise, the researcher fails to reject it. Failing to reject the null hypothesis does not prove it true. It means only that the data do not provide sufficient evidence against it, perhaps because the effect is small or the sample is too small to detect it.

Two types of error are possible. A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected, a false positive. Its probability equals the significance level alpha. A Type II error occurs when a false null hypothesis is not rejected, a false negative, and its probability is denoted beta. The power of a test, equal to one minus beta, is the probability of correctly detecting an effect when one exists. Power increases with larger sample sizes, larger true effects, lower variability, and higher alpha. Because reducing alpha makes it harder to reject the null hypothesis, there is a trade-off between the two error types for a fixed sample size.

P-values are widely misunderstood. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that the results occurred by chance alone. It is a statement about the data assuming the null hypothesis, not about the hypothesis given the data. A p-value of 0.03 does not mean there is a 97 percent probability that the alternative hypothesis is correct. In addition, the p-value does not measure the size or practical importance of an effect. With a very large sample, a trivial difference can produce a tiny p-value, while an important effect in a small study may not reach significance.

For these reasons, statisticians recommend reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside p-values. An effect size, such as a difference in means or a standardized mean difference, indicates how large the effect is, and a confidence interval shows the range of values compatible with the data. Together they allow readers to judge both statistical evidence and practical significance.

The rigid use of a 0.05 threshold has been criticized because it encourages dichotomous thinking, in which a p-value of 0.049 is treated as a discovery and 0.051 as a failure, although the evidence is almost identical. Problems also arise when researchers conduct many tests, try different analyses, or report only significant results, practices sometimes called p-hacking. Such practices inflate the rate of false positives and have contributed to concerns about the reproducibility of published research. Pre-registering hypotheses and analysis plans, correcting for multiple comparisons, and replicating findings are important safeguards. Used appropriately, hypothesis tests remain valuable tools, but they should support careful scientific judgement rather than replace it.
summary:
Hypothesis testing assesses whether observed patterns could plausibly result from random sampling variation. A null hypothesis, usually of no effect, is tested against an alternative that may be one- or two-sided and should be chosen before seeing the data. A test statistic such as z, t, chi-square, or F measures deviation from the null relative to sampling variability and has a known distribution under the null. The p-value is the probability, assuming the null is true, of results at least as extreme as those observed; if it is at or below the chosen significance level, often 0.05, the null is rejected, while failing to reject does not prove the null.

A Type I error (probability alpha) rejects a true null, and a Type II error (probability beta) misses a real effect; power (1 − beta) rises with larger samples and effects, lower variability, and higher alpha, so the errors trade off. A p-value is not the probability that the null is true and does not measure effect size or practical importance, so effect sizes and confidence intervals should be reported. Rigid 0.05 thresholds, multiple testing, and selective reporting (p-hacking) inflate false positives and harm reproducibility, which pre-registration, multiple-comparison corrections, and replication help prevent.

source_text:
Thermochemistry is the study of the heat absorbed or released during chemical reactions and physical changes. Most reactions involve a change in energy, because bonds are broken and new bonds are formed. These energy changes determine whether a fuel releases useful heat, how much cooling an industrial reactor requires, and how biological organisms obtain energy from food. Thermochemistry provides methods for measuring and calculating such changes even when they cannot be measured directly.

At constant pressure, the heat exchanged between a reacting system and its surroundings equals the change in enthalpy, written delta H. Enthalpy is a state function, which means that its value depends only on the current state of the system, defined by temperature, pressure, composition, and physical state, and not on the path by which that state was reached. A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings is exothermic and has a negative delta H; combustion of methane and the neutralization of acids by bases are examples. A reaction that absorbs heat is endothermic and has a positive delta H, as in the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate or the dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water.

Enthalpy changes are reported under standard conditions so that values from different sources can be compared. The standard state of a substance is its pure form at a pressure of one bar, and data are usually tabulated at 298 kelvin. The standard enthalpy of reaction, delta H degree, refers to the reaction occurring with all reactants and products in their standard states. Because enthalpy is an extensive property, its value depends on the amount of substance reacting. A thermochemical equation therefore shows the balanced chemical equation together with delta H for the amounts indicated, and the physical states of all species must be specified, because, for example, forming liquid water releases more heat than forming water vapour.

Thermochemical equations can be manipulated algebraically. If an equation is reversed, the sign of delta H is reversed. If the coefficients are multiplied by a factor, delta H is multiplied by the same factor. These rules follow directly from enthalpy being a state function and an extensive property.

Hess's law, formulated by Germain Hess in 1840, states that the total enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether the reaction occurs in one step or in several steps. It is a consequence of enthalpy being a state function. Hess's law is extremely useful because many enthalpy changes cannot be measured directly. For example, the formation of carbon monoxide from carbon and oxygen cannot be carried out cleanly, because some carbon dioxide always forms as well. However, the enthalpies of combustion of carbon to carbon dioxide and of carbon monoxide to carbon dioxide can both be measured. By writing the combustion of carbon, then subtracting the combustion of carbon monoxide, which means reversing that equation, the target reaction is obtained, and its enthalpy change is found by the same combination of enthalpy values.

A particularly important application uses standard enthalpies of formation. The standard enthalpy of formation, delta Hf degree, of a compound is the enthalpy change when one mole of the compound is formed from its elements in their standard states. By definition, the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its most stable form, such as oxygen gas or graphite, is zero. Using Hess's law, the standard enthalpy of any reaction can be calculated as the sum of the standard enthalpies of formation of the products, each multiplied by its stoichiometric coefficient, minus the corresponding sum for the reactants. Extensive tables of formation enthalpies therefore allow the enthalpy changes of thousands of reactions to be calculated without separate experiments.

Bond enthalpies provide another approach. The bond enthalpy is the energy required to break one mole of a particular type of bond in gaseous molecules. The enthalpy of a gas-phase reaction can be estimated as the total energy of bonds broken minus the total energy of bonds formed. Because tabulated bond enthalpies are averages over many different molecules, these estimates are approximate and less accurate than calculations based on formation enthalpies.

Experimental measurement of heat changes is carried out by calorimetry. In a simple coffee-cup calorimeter, a reaction in solution occurs at constant pressure, and the temperature change of the solution is measured. The heat absorbed or released is calculated from the mass of the solution, its specific heat capacity, and the temperature change, with corrections for heat absorbed by the container. A bomb calorimeter, used for combustion reactions, operates at constant volume and measures the change in internal energy, which can be converted to enthalpy. Combining calorimetric data with Hess's law forms the basis of the thermochemical tables used throughout chemistry and engineering.
summary:
Thermochemistry studies heat changes in reactions and physical processes. At constant pressure, the heat exchanged equals the enthalpy change ΔH, a state function that depends only on initial and final states; exothermic reactions such as combustion have negative ΔH, and endothermic reactions such as calcium carbonate decomposition have positive ΔH. Standard enthalpies refer to substances in standard states at 1 bar, usually tabulated at 298 K, and because enthalpy is extensive, thermochemical equations must specify amounts and physical states. Reversing an equation reverses the sign of ΔH, and multiplying coefficients multiplies ΔH.

Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change is the same whether a reaction occurs in one step or several, allowing unmeasurable enthalpies, such as carbon monoxide formation, to be calculated by combining measurable combustion reactions. Standard enthalpies of formation, zero for elements in their stable forms, give reaction enthalpies as the sum for products minus the sum for reactants, each weighted by stoichiometric coefficients. Average bond enthalpies provide approximate estimates for gas-phase reactions. Heat changes are measured by calorimetry, using constant-pressure coffee-cup calorimeters for solution reactions and constant-volume bomb calorimeters for combustion, and these data together with Hess's law underpin thermochemical tables.

In a multiprogramming system, several processes or threads compete for a finite set of resources, including memory regions, files, printers, database records, and locks protecting shared data. A deadlock occurs when a set of processes is permanently blocked because each process holds at least one resource and waits for another resource held by a different process in the same set. A simple example involves two processes and two locks: process P1 holds lock A and requests lock B, while process P2 holds lock B and requests lock A. Neither can proceed, and unless the system intervenes, both remain blocked indefinitely.

In 1971 Coffman and colleagues identified four conditions that must all hold simultaneously for a deadlock to occur. Mutual exclusion means that at least one resource can be used by only one process at a time. Hold and wait means that a process holding resources may request additional ones. No preemption means that resources cannot be forcibly taken from a process; they are released only voluntarily. Circular wait means that there is a cycle of processes in which each waits for a resource held by the next. Because all four conditions are necessary, eliminating any one of them prevents deadlock.

Resource allocation graphs provide a useful model. Processes and resource types are represented as nodes, a request edge points from a process to a resource it is waiting for, and an assignment edge points from a resource instance to the process holding it. If every resource type has a single instance, a cycle in the graph means that deadlock exists. If resource types have multiple instances, a cycle indicates that deadlock is possible but not certain, because another process might release an instance and break the cycle.

Operating systems handle deadlocks using four broad strategies. The first is deadlock prevention, which ensures that at least one of the four necessary conditions can never hold. Mutual exclusion usually cannot be removed for inherently non-shareable resources. Hold and wait can be eliminated by requiring processes to request all their resources at once before starting, or to release all resources before requesting new ones, but this reduces resource utilization and may cause starvation. No preemption can be relaxed by forcing a process that is denied a request to release the resources it holds, which works for resources whose state can be saved, such as CPU registers, but not for printers. Circular wait can be prevented by imposing a global ordering on resource types and requiring every process to request resources in increasing order. Lock ordering is the most practical prevention technique in software and is widely used in operating system kernels and multithreaded programs.

The second strategy is deadlock avoidance, which allows the four conditions in principle but uses advance information to ensure that the system never enters an unsafe state. Each process declares the maximum number of resources of each type it may need. A state is safe if there exists at least one sequence in which all processes can obtain their maximum needs and finish, each using resources released by those before it. Dijkstra's banker's algorithm, named by analogy with a banker who never lends money in a way that prevents satisfying all customers, grants a request only if the resulting state remains safe. It maintains matrices for allocation, maximum demand, and remaining need, together with a vector of available resources, and simulates whether all processes could complete. Avoidance offers better utilization than strict prevention, but it requires maximum demands to be known in advance, assumes a fixed number of processes and resources, and imposes computational overhead on every request, so it is rarely used in general-purpose operating systems.

The third strategy is detection and recovery. The system allows deadlocks to occur, periodically runs a detection algorithm, and recovers when a deadlock is found. For single-instance resources, detection reduces to finding cycles in a wait-for graph, which contains only process nodes and edges showing which process waits for which. For multiple instances, an algorithm similar to the safety check of the banker's algorithm determines whether some processes can never finish. Recovery options include terminating all deadlocked processes, terminating them one at a time until the cycle is broken, or preempting resources and rolling processes back to an earlier checkpoint. Choosing which process to terminate or roll back involves considering priority, computation already performed, and resources held, while avoiding repeatedly selecting the same victim, which would cause starvation. Database management systems commonly use detection and recovery: when transactions deadlock on record locks, one transaction is aborted and rolled back so that the others can continue.

The fourth strategy is to ignore the problem, sometimes called the ostrich approach. Many general-purpose operating systems do not attempt to handle all possible deadlocks in user applications, because deadlocks are relatively rare and the cost of prevention or avoidance would reduce performance for all programs. Responsibility then falls on application developers, who use techniques such as consistent lock ordering, timeouts on lock acquisition, and careful design of concurrent code.

Deadlock should be distinguished from related problems. Livelock occurs when processes continually change state in response to one another without making progress, as when two processes repeatedly back off and retry at the same moments. Starvation occurs when a process waits indefinitely because others are repeatedly favoured, even though the system as a whole is not deadlocked. Good concurrency design must address all three.
summary:
A deadlock occurs when processes are permanently blocked because each holds a resource and waits for another held by a process in the same set. Coffman's four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Resource allocation graphs model requests and assignments; with single-instance resources a cycle means deadlock, while with multiple instances it means deadlock is only possible.

Prevention ensures a condition cannot hold: hold and wait can be removed by requesting all resources at once, no preemption relaxed for saveable resources, and circular wait prevented by global resource ordering, the most practical technique. Avoidance, exemplified by Dijkstra's banker's algorithm, uses declared maximum needs to grant requests only if the system remains in a safe state, but requires advance knowledge and adds overhead, so it is rarely used generally. Detection and recovery allow deadlocks, detect them through wait-for graph cycles or safety-style algorithms, and recover by terminating processes or preempting resources with rollback, as databases do by aborting transactions. Many operating systems ignore application deadlocks, leaving developers to use lock ordering and timeouts. Deadlock differs from livelock, where processes keep changing state without progress, and starvation, where a process is indefinitely passed over.

Many signals encountered in electrical engineering are periodic, repeating exactly after a fixed interval called the period. Examples include the alternating supply voltage, the output of oscillators, the square waves used as digital clocks, and the waveforms produced by rectifiers and switching converters. The Fourier series, introduced by Joseph Fourier in his studies of heat conduction in the early nineteenth century, shows that almost any periodic signal can be represented as a sum of sinusoids whose frequencies are integer multiples of a fundamental frequency. This representation allows engineers to analyse signals and systems in the frequency domain.

For a periodic signal with period T, the fundamental frequency is f0 equal to one divided by T, or in angular terms omega0 equal to two pi divided by T. The trigonometric Fourier series expresses the signal as a constant term, a0, plus an infinite sum of cosine and sine terms at frequencies n omega0, where n is a positive integer. The constant a0 equals the average or DC value of the signal over one period. The coefficients of the cosine terms, an, and the sine terms, bn, are obtained by integrating the product of the signal with the corresponding cosine or sine over one period and scaling the result. The component at the fundamental frequency is called the first harmonic, and the components at twice, three times, and higher multiples are the second, third, and higher harmonics.

An equivalent compact form combines each pair of cosine and sine terms into a single cosine with an amplitude and a phase angle. The amplitude of the nth harmonic equals the square root of an squared plus bn squared, and the phase depends on the ratio of the two coefficients. A further form, the exponential Fourier series, represents the signal as a sum of complex exponentials with complex coefficients cn for both positive and negative values of n. Although negative frequencies have no separate physical meaning, the exponential form is mathematically convenient and leads directly to the Fourier transform used for non-periodic signals.

Symmetry simplifies the calculation of coefficients. If a signal has even symmetry, meaning it is unchanged when reflected about the vertical axis, all sine coefficients are zero and the series contains only cosine terms and possibly a DC term. If it has odd symmetry, meaning it changes sign when reflected, the DC term and all cosine coefficients are zero and only sine terms remain. A signal with half-wave symmetry, in which the second half of each period is the negative of the first half, contains only odd harmonics. A symmetric square wave, for example, can be written as a sum of sine terms at the fundamental and its odd harmonics, with amplitudes decreasing in proportion to one divided by the harmonic number.

The Fourier series leads naturally to the concept of a frequency spectrum. The amplitude spectrum plots the amplitude of each harmonic against frequency, and the phase spectrum plots the corresponding phase angles. Because a periodic signal contains only discrete frequencies, its spectrum consists of separate lines, called a line spectrum. The spectrum reveals features that are difficult to see in the time domain. A pure sinusoid has a single line, a square wave has lines at odd harmonics that fall off slowly, and a triangular wave has odd harmonics that decrease much more rapidly, in proportion to one divided by the square of the harmonic number. In general, signals with abrupt changes or discontinuities contain stronger high-frequency components, while smooth signals have spectra concentrated at low frequencies.

The convergence of the series has a notable feature. At a discontinuity, such as the jump in a square wave, the series converges to the midpoint of the jump. Near the discontinuity, a partial sum with a finite number of terms overshoots the true value by about nine percent of the jump, and this overshoot does not disappear as more terms are added, although it becomes concentrated closer to the discontinuity. This behaviour is known as the Gibbs phenomenon.

Parseval's theorem connects the time and frequency domains in terms of power. It states that the average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of the powers of its individual harmonic components, together with the power of the DC component. This allows engineers to determine how much of a signal's power lies within a particular frequency band, which is important in communication systems and in measuring distortion.

Fourier series have many engineering applications. When a periodic signal is applied to a linear time-invariant system, each harmonic passes through the system independently, scaled and phase-shifted according to the system's frequency response at that frequency. The output can therefore be found by adding the responses to each harmonic. This principle is used to analyse filters and to design circuits that remove unwanted components. In power systems, nonlinear loads such as rectifiers and variable-speed drives draw non-sinusoidal currents containing harmonics, which cause additional heating, interference, and distortion. Total harmonic distortion, defined as the ratio of the root-mean-square value of all harmonic components to that of the fundamental, is used to quantify waveform quality and to set limits on harmonic emissions.
summary:
The Fourier series represents a periodic signal as a sum of sinusoids at integer multiples of its fundamental frequency f0 = 1/T. The trigonometric form contains a DC term a0, equal to the average value, plus cosine and sine terms whose coefficients are found by integration over one period; the components are the fundamental and higher harmonics. Equivalent forms use amplitude-phase cosines, with amplitude √(an² + bn²), or complex exponentials, which lead to the Fourier transform. Symmetry simplifies analysis: even signals contain only cosines, odd signals only sines, and half-wave symmetric signals only odd harmonics, as in a square wave whose odd harmonics fall as 1/n.

Periodic signals have discrete line spectra showing harmonic amplitudes and phases; sharp transitions produce strong high-frequency content, while smooth signals, such as triangular waves with harmonics falling as 1/n², concentrate energy at low frequencies. At discontinuities, the series converges to the midpoint and partial sums overshoot by about 9% (the Gibbs phenomenon). Parseval's theorem equates average signal power with the sum of harmonic and DC powers. In linear systems each harmonic is scaled and shifted by the frequency response, enabling filter analysis, and in power systems harmonics from nonlinear loads cause heating and distortion, quantified by total harmonic distortion.

When a building, embankment, or storage tank is placed on the ground, the soil beneath it compresses and the structure settles. In sands and gravels, most settlement occurs quickly because water can drain easily from the pores. In saturated clays, however, settlement may continue for months, years, or even decades. This slow, time-dependent compression of saturated fine-grained soil caused by the gradual expulsion of pore water is called consolidation. Estimating both the magnitude and the rate of consolidation settlement is essential for designing foundations that perform acceptably, because excessive or uneven settlement can crack walls, tilt structures, and damage pipes and pavements.

The mechanism of consolidation can be understood through the spring and piston analogy proposed by Karl Terzaghi. Imagine a cylinder filled with water, containing a spring that represents the soil skeleton and a piston with a small valve that represents the low permeability of clay. When a load is applied suddenly, water cannot escape immediately, so the water carries the entire load and its pressure rises above its initial hydrostatic value. This increase is called excess pore water pressure. As water gradually drains through the valve, the excess pore pressure decreases, the spring compresses, and the load is progressively transferred to the spring. Consolidation is complete when the excess pore pressure has fully dissipated and the soil skeleton carries the entire additional load as an increase in effective stress.

Total settlement of a foundation on clay is commonly divided into three components. Immediate or elastic settlement occurs as the load is applied and results from the distortion of the soil without significant volume change. Primary consolidation settlement results from the dissipation of excess pore water pressure and the associated decrease in void ratio. Secondary compression, sometimes called creep, continues after primary consolidation is complete and results from the gradual rearrangement of soil particles under constant effective stress. In soft and organic clays, secondary compression can be significant.

The compressibility of clay is determined in the laboratory using the oedometer, or one-dimensional consolidation, test. An undisturbed specimen is placed in a rigid ring that prevents lateral deformation, with porous stones above and below to allow drainage. Loads are applied in increments, typically each double the previous one, and the vertical deformation is recorded over time for each increment. The results are plotted as void ratio against the logarithm of effective stress. This curve usually shows a relatively flat initial portion, called the recompression range, followed by a steeper, approximately straight portion, called the virgin compression line. The slope of the virgin compression line is the compression index, Cc, while the slope of the recompression and unloading portions is the recompression or swell index, Cr, which is much smaller.

An important concept derived from this curve is the preconsolidation pressure, the maximum effective stress that the soil has experienced in its history. If the current effective stress equals the preconsolidation pressure, the clay is normally consolidated. If the current stress is lower, because of past loading by glaciers, erosion of overlying soil, or fluctuations of groundwater, the clay is overconsolidated, and the ratio of preconsolidation pressure to current stress is called the overconsolidation ratio. Overconsolidated clays are much less compressible for loads that keep the stress below the preconsolidation pressure, because they follow the flatter recompression curve.

The magnitude of primary consolidation settlement for a clay layer is calculated from the change in void ratio. For a normally consolidated clay, the settlement equals the compression index multiplied by the layer thickness, divided by one plus the initial void ratio, multiplied by the logarithm of the ratio of final to initial effective stress. For an overconsolidated clay, the recompression index is used for the portion of stress increase below the preconsolidation pressure and the compression index for any portion above it. The stress increase at the centre of the clay layer is estimated using methods such as the Boussinesq solution or simpler approximations, since the added stress decreases with depth beneath a loaded area.

The rate of consolidation is described by Terzaghi's one-dimensional consolidation theory. The key parameter is the coefficient of consolidation, cv, which depends on the soil's permeability and compressibility and is determined from the time-settlement curves of the oedometer test. The time required to reach a given degree of consolidation is proportional to the square of the drainage path length divided by cv. The drainage path is the maximum distance water must travel to reach a permeable boundary; for a clay layer drained at both top and bottom, it is half the layer thickness. Because time depends on the square of this distance, doubling the drainage path quadruples the consolidation time. A dimensionless time factor relates elapsed time to the average degree of consolidation.

When predicted consolidation times are too long for a construction schedule, engineers may accelerate the process. Preloading applies a temporary surcharge, often an earth fill, so that much of the settlement occurs before the permanent structure is built. Prefabricated vertical drains, also called wick drains, inserted into the clay shorten the drainage path by allowing water to flow horizontally to the drains, greatly reducing consolidation time. These techniques are widely used for embankments, reclaimed land, and port facilities built on soft clay deposits.
summary:
Consolidation is the slow, time-dependent compression of saturated clay as pore water is gradually expelled under load, and it can cause settlement lasting years that damages structures. Terzaghi's spring-and-piston analogy shows that a sudden load is first carried by excess pore water pressure, which dissipates as water drains, transferring the load to the soil skeleton as increased effective stress. Total settlement includes immediate elastic settlement, primary consolidation from pore pressure dissipation, and secondary compression or creep, which is important in soft and organic clays.

Oedometer tests on confined specimens give void ratio versus log effective stress curves, with a steep virgin compression line of slope Cc and a flatter recompression range of slope Cr. The preconsolidation pressure is the maximum past effective stress; clays are normally consolidated when current stress equals it and overconsolidated when lower, with an overconsolidation ratio that reduces compressibility below that pressure. Primary settlement is calculated from Cc or Cr, layer thickness, initial void ratio, and the logarithmic stress increase, estimated at mid-layer. Terzaghi's theory gives the rate through the coefficient of consolidation cv, with time proportional to the square of the drainage path, half the thickness for double drainage. Preloading with surcharge and prefabricated vertical drains accelerate consolidation for embankments and reclaimed land.

Gears are toothed wheels that transmit motion and power between rotating shafts. They are found in vehicle gearboxes, wind turbines, machine tools, clocks, and countless other machines. Compared with belts and chains, gears provide a positive drive without slip, can transmit large torques in a compact space, and maintain an exact speed ratio. Their design requires an understanding of tooth geometry, the kinematics of meshing gears, and the arrangement of gears in trains.

Gears are classified according to the relative position of their shafts. Spur gears have straight teeth parallel to the axis of rotation and connect parallel shafts; they are simple and efficient but can be noisy at high speeds because each tooth engages suddenly across its full width. Helical gears also connect parallel shafts, but their teeth are cut at an angle to the axis, so engagement begins at one end of the tooth and spreads gradually, producing smoother and quieter operation. The inclined teeth, however, generate an axial thrust that must be carried by the bearings; double helical or herringbone gears cancel this thrust. Bevel gears connect intersecting shafts, usually at right angles, and worm gears connect non-intersecting perpendicular shafts, providing large speed reductions in a single stage, though with lower efficiency because of sliding between the worm and wheel.

Several geometric terms describe gear teeth. The pitch circle is an imaginary circle on which two meshing gears roll without slipping, and its diameter is the pitch diameter. The circular pitch is the distance between corresponding points on adjacent teeth measured along the pitch circle. In metric practice, tooth size is expressed by the module, equal to the pitch diameter divided by the number of teeth, while in the inch system the diametral pitch, the number of teeth per inch of pitch diameter, is used. Two gears can mesh correctly only if they have the same module. The addendum is the radial height of a tooth above the pitch circle, and the dedendum is the depth below it; the dedendum is slightly larger than the addendum to provide clearance at the root.

Correct meshing requires that the gears maintain a constant angular velocity ratio throughout engagement. This requirement is expressed by the fundamental law of gearing, which states that the common normal to the tooth profiles at the point of contact must always pass through a fixed point on the line joining the centres, called the pitch point. Profiles that satisfy this law are called conjugate. The involute curve, traced by the end of a taut string unwound from a circle called the base circle, is used for almost all modern gears. Involute teeth have the important advantage that small changes in centre distance, caused by manufacturing tolerances or bearing wear, do not affect the velocity ratio. The angle between the line of action and the tangent to the pitch circles is the pressure angle, commonly 20 degrees in modern standards.

For a pair of gears, the speed ratio is inversely proportional to the numbers of teeth. If a driving pinion with 20 teeth meshes with a driven gear with 60 teeth, the gear rotates at one third of the pinion speed, and, neglecting losses, the torque on the output shaft is three times the input torque, since power is the product of torque and angular speed. The two gears rotate in opposite directions. The contact ratio, the average number of tooth pairs in contact, should exceed one, typically 1.4 to 1.8, so that a new pair of teeth begins to engage before the previous pair separates, ensuring smooth transmission.

Interference is a geometric problem that occurs when the tip of a tooth on one gear contacts the non-involute portion of the mating tooth below the base circle. It can cause undercutting during manufacture, which weakens the tooth root. Interference is more likely when a pinion has very few teeth. For standard 20-degree full-depth teeth, the minimum number of teeth on a pinion to avoid undercutting when meshing with a rack is about 17. Profile shifting, in which the cutting tool is displaced during manufacture, can allow fewer teeth.

Gear trains combine several gears to achieve large speed ratios, change direction, or connect distant shafts. In a simple gear train, each shaft carries one gear, and the overall ratio depends only on the first and last gears; intermediate idler gears change the direction of rotation without changing the ratio. In a compound gear train, some shafts carry two gears rigidly connected, so the overall ratio equals the product of the ratios of each meshing pair, allowing large reductions in a compact arrangement. A reverted gear train is a compound train in which the input and output shafts are coaxial, as in some vehicle gearboxes.

Epicyclic or planetary gear trains contain gears whose axes move. A typical arrangement includes a central sun gear, several planet gears that mesh with the sun and rotate on a carrier, and an outer ring gear with internal teeth. By holding one of the three members stationary and driving another, different speed ratios are obtained. Planetary trains offer high torque capacity, compact size, and coaxial shafts, which is why they are used in automatic transmissions, hybrid vehicle drives, and wind turbine gearboxes. Their speed ratios are analysed using relative motion, for example with the tabular method or the Willis equation.

Gear design must also consider strength and durability. Teeth may fail by bending fatigue at the root, by surface fatigue such as pitting caused by repeated contact stresses, or by wear and scoring when lubrication is inadequate. The Lewis equation provides a basic estimate of bending stress, and contact stress is evaluated using Hertzian contact theory, both modified by factors for dynamic loading, misalignment, and material properties in standards such as those of the American Gear Manufacturers Association and ISO.
summary:
Gears transmit motion and power between shafts with a positive, slip-free drive, high torque capacity, and exact speed ratios. Spur gears connect parallel shafts simply but can be noisy; helical gears engage gradually and run quieter but create axial thrust, cancelled in herringbone gears; bevel gears connect intersecting shafts; and worm gears give large reductions between perpendicular non-intersecting shafts at lower efficiency. Key geometry includes the pitch circle and diameter, circular pitch, module (pitch diameter divided by teeth, equal for meshing gears), diametral pitch, addendum, and dedendum.

The fundamental law of gearing requires the contact normal to pass through the fixed pitch point for a constant velocity ratio; involute profiles satisfy it and tolerate centre-distance changes, usually with a 20° pressure angle. The speed ratio is inversely proportional to tooth numbers, with torque increasing as speed falls, and a contact ratio of about 1.4–1.8 ensures smooth engagement. Interference and undercutting occur with very few pinion teeth, about 17 being the minimum for standard 20° teeth, unless profile shifting is used. Simple trains use idlers to change direction, compound trains multiply stage ratios, reverted trains have coaxial shafts, and planetary trains with sun, planets, carrier, and ring offer compact high-torque ratios. Design checks bending fatigue (Lewis equation), contact stress and pitting (Hertzian theory), and wear using AGMA or ISO factors.

Spinning is the process of converting fibres into yarn, a continuous strand strong enough to be woven, knitted, or sewn. Staple fibres, such as cotton, wool, and cut synthetic fibres, have limited length, so they must be aligned, drawn into a fine strand, and twisted together to create cohesion. Ring spinning, developed in the nineteenth century, remains the most widely used method for producing staple yarns, particularly fine and high-quality cotton yarns, because it can spin a very wide range of counts and gives yarns with excellent strength and structure.

Before ring spinning, fibres pass through a sequence of preparatory processes. In blowroom operations, compressed bales are opened into small tufts, mixed for uniformity, and cleaned of trash such as seeds and leaf fragments. Carding further opens the tufts into individual fibres, removes remaining impurities and very short fibres, and forms a soft rope-like strand called a card sliver, although the fibres in it are not well aligned. Drawing combines several slivers and stretches them between rollers moving at different speeds, which straightens and parallelizes the fibres and improves evenness by averaging irregularities. For fine, high-quality yarns, combing is added to remove short fibres and neps, small tangled knots of fibre. Finally, the roving frame, or speed frame, draws the sliver into a thinner strand called roving and inserts a small amount of twist to give it enough strength to be wound onto a bobbin and fed to the ring frame.

On the ring spinning frame, the roving is fed into a drafting system, usually consisting of three pairs of rollers. Each successive pair rotates faster than the one before, so the strand is stretched, or drafted, reducing its linear density to that of the final yarn. Total drafts on modern ring frames are commonly in the range of about 20 to 50. Aprons, thin belts running around the middle rollers, control the movement of short fibres during drafting, which would otherwise float uncontrolled between roller pairs and create irregularities.

After drafting, the thin ribbon of fibres emerges from the front rollers and is immediately twisted. The yarn passes through a guide, then through a small C-shaped metal clip called a traveller, which runs freely around a steel ring surrounding a rotating spindle. The spindle carries a bobbin on which the yarn is wound. As the spindle rotates at high speed, often 15,000 to 25,000 revolutions per minute, the yarn drags the traveller around the ring. Because of friction and air resistance, the traveller lags slightly behind the spindle, and this difference in speed winds the yarn onto the bobbin. At the same time, each rotation of the traveller inserts one turn of twist into the yarn. The ring rail moves up and down to build the yarn package in a regular shape.

Twist is a key factor in yarn properties. Twist binds the fibres together by creating radial pressure that increases friction between them, so up to a certain level, more twist increases strength. Beyond an optimum, further twist reduces strength because fibres become increasingly inclined to the yarn axis and are subjected to additional stresses. The amount of twist is described by turns per metre or turns per inch and is often expressed through the twist multiplier, which relates twist to yarn count so that yarns of different fineness can be compared. Twist also affects handle, softness, lustre, and appearance: low-twist yarns are soft and bulky, suitable for knitted fabrics, while higher-twist yarns are stronger and used for warp yarns in weaving. Twist direction is designated as S or Z, depending on whether the fibre spirals match the central part of the letter.

During twisting, the fibre strand emerging from the front rollers forms a small triangular region called the spinning triangle. Fibres at the edges of this triangle are not fully integrated into the yarn and can form protruding ends, contributing to hairiness. Compact spinning modifies the ring frame by using suction or mechanical condensing devices to narrow the fibre strand before twisting, nearly eliminating the spinning triangle. Compact yarns are less hairy, stronger, and more even, and they are used for premium fabrics.

The main limitation of ring spinning is productivity. Because the spindle must rotate once for each turn of twist and the traveller speed is limited by frictional heating and wear, production speed per spindle is relatively low, and frequent doffing, the removal of full bobbins, is required. Energy consumption is also significant. Higher-productivity methods such as rotor and air-jet spinning have therefore replaced ring spinning for some coarser counts. Nevertheless, ring spinning remains dominant for fine and medium counts and for applications requiring the best combination of strength, evenness, and fabric quality.

Quality control in ring spinning involves monitoring yarn count, twist, strength, elongation, evenness, imperfections such as thin places, thick places, and neps, and hairiness. Instruments measure unevenness using capacitance sensors and report the coefficient of variation of mass along the yarn. Electronic yarn clearers on winding machines remove objectionable faults and splice the yarn ends together.
summary:
Ring spinning is the most widely used method for producing staple yarns, especially fine, strong cotton yarns. Preparation includes blowroom opening, mixing, and cleaning; carding to separate fibres and form sliver; drawing to parallelize fibres and improve evenness; optional combing to remove short fibres and neps for fine yarns; and the roving frame, which produces a lightly twisted roving. On the ring frame, a three-roller drafting system with aprons reduces the roving to yarn fineness, typically with drafts of about 20–50.

The yarn passes through a traveller that circulates on a ring around a spindle rotating at about 15,000–25,000 rpm; the traveller's lag winds yarn onto the bobbin while each rotation inserts one turn of twist, and the moving ring rail builds the package. Twist increases strength up to an optimum, is expressed as turns per metre or a twist multiplier, influences softness and appearance, and has S or Z direction. Fibres at the edges of the spinning triangle cause hairiness, which compact spinning reduces to give stronger, more even yarn. Ring spinning's low productivity, frequent doffing, and energy use have led to rotor and air-jet spinning for coarser counts, though ring yarns dominate fine and medium counts. Quality control measures count, twist, strength, elongation, evenness, imperfections, and hairiness, with electronic clearers removing faults.

source_text:
Ophthalmic dosage forms are pharmaceutical preparations intended for application to the eye or its surrounding tissues. They are used to treat conditions such as glaucoma, bacterial and viral infections, allergic conjunctivitis, inflammation after surgery, and dry eye disease. Formulating medicines for the eye is challenging, because the eye is a sensitive organ with efficient protective mechanisms that rapidly remove applied drugs, and because any preparation must be sterile, comfortable, and non-irritating.

The anatomy and physiology of the eye strongly influence drug delivery. When a drop is instilled into the lower conjunctival sac, it mixes with the tear film, but the sac can hold only about 7 to 10 microlitres in addition to the normal tear volume, whereas a typical eye drop is 30 to 50 microlitres. Much of the instilled volume therefore overflows onto the cheek or drains through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity, from which it may be absorbed into the systemic circulation. Reflex tearing and blinking further dilute and wash away the drug. As a result, only a small fraction of a topically applied dose, often less than five percent, reaches the internal tissues of the eye.

The cornea is the main barrier to drug penetration into the anterior chamber. It consists of three principal layers with contrasting properties. The outer epithelium is lipophilic and has tight junctions, the middle stroma is hydrophilic and makes up most of the corneal thickness, and the inner endothelium is a single cell layer. A drug must therefore have a balance of lipophilic and hydrophilic properties to cross all layers efficiently. Many ophthalmic drugs are weak bases or acids whose degree of ionization, and therefore penetration, depends on pH.

Eye drops, or ophthalmic solutions, are the most common dosage form because they are easy to administer and do not interfere with vision. Formulation requires attention to several properties. Sterility is essential, since contaminated eye products can cause serious infections; solutions are sterilized by filtration or by heat when the drug is stable. Multi-dose containers contain antimicrobial preservatives, such as benzalkonium chloride, to prevent contamination after opening. Benzalkonium chloride is effective but can damage the corneal epithelium with long-term use, which has led to preservative-free single-dose units and specialized multi-dose bottles for patients who use drops frequently.

Tonicity and pH also affect comfort and stability. Tears are approximately isotonic with 0.9 percent sodium chloride, and solutions with tonicity roughly equivalent to 0.6 to 2.0 percent sodium chloride are generally tolerated. Tonicity agents such as sodium chloride or mannitol are added when needed. Tear fluid has a pH of about 7.4 and some buffering capacity. Although a pH close to that of tears is most comfortable, the pH chosen is often a compromise between comfort, drug solubility, and chemical stability, so many products use a weak buffer that tears can quickly neutralize. Viscosity-enhancing agents, such as hydroxypropyl methylcellulose or polyvinyl alcohol, increase the residence time of the solution on the eye surface and are also used alone as artificial tears.

Ophthalmic suspensions are used for drugs that are poorly soluble in water, such as some corticosteroids. Particle size must be very small, typically below about ten micrometres, to avoid irritation and to ensure uniform dosing, and patients must shake the container before use. Ophthalmic ointments, usually based on white petrolatum and mineral oil, provide prolonged contact time and protect the eye surface, and they are often used at night because they blur vision. Gels offer a compromise between solutions and ointments.

Several approaches have been developed to overcome rapid precorneal elimination. In situ gelling systems are liquids that turn into gels on contact with the eye in response to temperature, pH, or ions present in tears; gellan gum, for instance, gels in the presence of tear cations. Mucoadhesive polymers interact with the mucin layer of the tear film and prolong residence. Ocular inserts are solid or semi-solid devices placed in the conjunctival sac that release drug at a controlled rate. Nanoparticles, liposomes, and nanoemulsions can improve the penetration and retention of poorly soluble drugs. For diseases of the retina and other posterior segment tissues, which topical drops rarely reach in therapeutic concentrations, drugs are delivered by intravitreal injections or biodegradable implants.

Patients also influence the effectiveness of ophthalmic therapy. Correct technique involves washing hands, pulling down the lower eyelid to form a pocket, instilling one drop without touching the eye or lashes with the dropper tip, and closing the eye gently for about one to two minutes. Pressing on the inner corner of the eye, called nasolacrimal occlusion, reduces drainage into the nose, increasing ocular absorption and decreasing systemic side effects. When several eye medicines are prescribed, an interval of about five minutes between drops prevents the first from being washed out by the second.
summary:
Ophthalmic dosage forms treat conditions such as glaucoma, infections, allergy, inflammation, and dry eye, but must be sterile, comfortable, and non-irritating, and the eye rapidly removes applied drugs. The conjunctival sac holds only about 7–10 µL beyond normal tears, so much of a 30–50 µL drop overflows or drains through the nasolacrimal duct, and tearing and blinking dilute it; often less than 5% reaches internal tissues. The cornea's lipophilic epithelium, hydrophilic stroma, and endothelium require drugs with balanced solubility, with ionization dependent on pH.

Eye drops require sterility, preservatives such as benzalkonium chloride in multi-dose containers (with preservative-free options because of corneal toxicity), tonicity roughly equivalent to 0.6–2.0% sodium chloride, and a pH balancing comfort, solubility, and stability with weak buffering; viscosity agents prolong contact. Suspensions need particles below about 10 µm and shaking, ointments prolong contact but blur vision, and gels are intermediate. In situ gelling systems, mucoadhesive polymers, ocular inserts, and nanocarriers prolong residence or improve penetration, while intravitreal injections and implants reach the posterior segment. Correct patient technique, nasolacrimal occlusion, and spacing multiple drops by about five minutes improve effectiveness and reduce systemic effects.

source_text:
Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites. They consist of a genome of either DNA or RNA enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid, and some viruses are further surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from host membranes. Viruses lack the ribosomes, enzymes, and energy-generating systems needed for independent metabolism, so they can replicate only inside living host cells, using the cell's machinery to make new virus particles. Although viruses differ greatly in structure and genome type, their replication can be described as a series of common stages: attachment, entry, uncoating, genome replication and gene expression, assembly, and release.

Attachment, also called adsorption, is the specific binding of viral surface proteins to receptor molecules on the host cell. Receptor specificity largely determines host range, the species a virus can infect, and tissue tropism, the cell types it targets within a host. Human immunodeficiency virus, for example, binds the CD4 protein and a co-receptor found mainly on certain immune cells, while influenza virus binds sialic acid-containing molecules on respiratory epithelial cells. Because attachment is the first essential step, it is a target for neutralizing antibodies and some antiviral drugs.

Entry follows attachment. Enveloped viruses may enter by fusion of their envelope with the plasma membrane, releasing the capsid directly into the cytoplasm. Alternatively, many viruses are taken up by receptor-mediated endocytosis, enclosed in an endosome; the acidic pH inside the endosome then triggers conformational changes in viral proteins that cause fusion of the viral envelope with the endosomal membrane or, for non-enveloped viruses, disruption of the membrane. Uncoating is the release of the viral genome from the capsid, which may occur at the cell membrane, in the cytoplasm, or at the nuclear pore, depending on the virus.

The strategy of genome replication and gene expression depends on the type of nucleic acid. All viruses must produce messenger RNA that host ribosomes can translate. The Baltimore classification groups viruses into seven classes according to how they generate mRNA. Double-stranded DNA viruses, such as herpesviruses, usually replicate in the nucleus using host or viral DNA polymerases and transcribe mRNA with host RNA polymerase. Positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses, such as poliovirus and coronaviruses, have genomes that can function directly as mRNA; they are translated on entry to produce viral proteins, including an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase that copies the genome. Negative-sense RNA viruses, such as influenza and rabies viruses, must carry their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion, because their genome must first be transcribed into complementary positive-sense mRNA. Retroviruses, such as HIV, carry reverse transcriptase, which copies their RNA genome into DNA; this DNA is integrated into the host chromosome by the viral enzyme integrase and then transcribed by host enzymes. Because host cells do not possess RNA-dependent polymerases or reverse transcriptase, these viral enzymes are important targets for antiviral drugs.

Viral gene expression is often temporally regulated. Early genes typically encode proteins needed for genome replication and for modifying host cell functions, whereas late genes encode structural proteins required for building new virions.
